Causal Feature Engineering and Learned Residual Evidence for Online Structural Break Detection

Author: Joseph (Koen) Engels, Independent researcher
Technical competition report · Final · revised 1 November 2026

Abstract

The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) supports the independent research institute ADIA Lab. I study causal structural-break detection in its Real Time Challenge with CrunchDAO. The task requires a score after every online observation and evaluates cross-sectional ranking using time-stratified area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (TS-AUC).

My selected submission combines engineered statistical features, autoregressive residual representations and a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) student trained on nested cross-fitted soft labels. It achieved a recorded public leaderboard score of 0.6191 and a final private score of 0.6196 (rank 239 of 819 scored models; winner 0.6935).

Subsequent offline research examines learned normal-process models, neural and pretrained forecasting representations, nested width selection, temporal blending and sequential residual evidence. On matched search folds, a combination using a selected-width gated recurrent unit (GRU) null model scores 0.622489, and adding sequential mean, energy and lag-product evidence raises the mean to 0.623224. The incremental gain is positive in nine of fifteen fold–seed cells, but fails all five two-half bootstrap gates for every tree seed against the preceding combination. Temporal analysis locates most of the additional gain before online step 100, with a regression between steps 100 and 249. A subsequent 8,000-series likelihood search for generalized autoregressive score models with Student-t innovations (GAS-t) raises its matched blend from 0.619810 to 0.620676, but fails all 105 declared gates and remains below the GRU combinations.

I document scorer and leakage corrections, distinguish search evidence from fixed-holdout confirmation, and report unsuccessful methods alongside promising candidates. As of 28 October 2026, submission 46 remains the selected recorded public result; the competition run window is closed, and neither sequential residual evidence nor the GAS-t blend has received a new public score or a registered holdout confirmation. The results support complementary residual representations as a research direction, while leaving replacement of the selected submission unconfirmed.

Keywords: online structural break detection; time-stratified AUC; feature engineering; nested cross-fitting; soft labels; learned null models; stacking; sequential evidence; cluster bootstrap.

1 Introduction

Structural changes can invalidate a forecasting or monitoring model without producing a single extreme observation. A detector must identify sustained changes in location, scale or dependence while retaining sensitivity to weak transitions. The difficulty increases when observations arrive sequentially and the change location is unknown.

ADIA Lab is an independent institute supported by the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA). Its challenge with CrunchDAO in 2026 imposes this online setting: historical observations are available initially, but each online score must be returned before the next observation is revealed [1]. Its mechanics differ from the 2025 competition, where both segments were available and the candidate boundary was given [2]. Consequently, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) figures from the previous competition cannot be used as numerical baselines for the current TS-AUC task.

Previous competition write-ups illustrate the value of diverse statistical features and ensembles [3]. My report follows that technical solution-report form but addresses the online constraint. I contribute: (i) an audited account of the selected feature-based submission; (ii) matched comparisons of learned-null and foundation-model routes; (iii) a causal sequential-residual representation evaluated with nested feature construction; and (iv) a failure analysis separating average improvements from statistical acceptance. I do not claim a new globally optimal detector or an exhaustive architecture benchmark.

1.1 Related work and the previous edition

The 2025 winning-team solution report [3] and the previous-edition task documentation [2] provide comparative context. The winning report combines several statistical feature representations through tree-based stacking. It motivates examining complementary representations, but its known-boundary, complete-segment setting differs from causal monitoring at an unknown change location. I therefore discuss its architecture rather than using its scores as baselines. This comparison does not establish that every previous-edition paper was reviewed or that those publications guided all earlier experiments.

2 Problem formulation and data

2.1 Data supplied by the organizers

I received the ADIA Lab–CrunchDAO Real Time dataset, described in the official dataset documentation [1]. The files are obtained through the competition Hub and its participant setup. My local copy contains 10,000 labelled training series and a separate labelled reduced test set of 100 series. The full public and private test sets each contain 10,000 series and are evaluated on the platform; their labels are unavailable to my inference code.

The organizers describe a mixture of real-world and synthetic data-generating processes (DGPs), with possible changes in location, scale, distributional shape or dependence. The supplied files do not identify each series' exact DGP, original source domain or whether it is real or synthetic. This limits what I can infer about the collection: financial and sensor processes are possible interpretations, not established provenance. My retrospective break-type analysis is a diagnostic constructed from observations, not organizer-supplied DGP metadata.

Each series has a break-free historical reference, typically 1,000–5,000 observations, followed by an online segment of 10–1,000 observations. A series has at most one break, located somewhere in the online segment, or no break. Values are standardized separately for each series using its historical mean and standard deviation; those normalization parameters remain fixed during online inference [1]. In the supplied Parquet files, the series identifier and observation index form an (id, time) index, and period distinguishes history (1) from online observations (2).

Supplied local fileContents and role

y_train.parquetBinary target for every online training observation: zero before a break, one from the break onward
y_train_index.parquetSeries-level break position: tau_index counts from zero within the online segment; a negative index denotes no break; tau is also supplied

Table 1. Organizer-supplied training and reduced-test files used in this study. The file schemas were checked against the actual Parquet metadata. These are input data, distinct from the feature caches and retrospective analyses generated during my research.

No forward-looking inference code is permitted: the detector must return its score for the current observation before receiving the next one, and the online iterator cannot be reread [1]. Consequently, a prediction may use the complete historical segment and the online prefix received so far, but no later online values, normalization over the complete online segment, or evaluation break labels. Training labels supervise fitting; retrospective break locations and types support evaluation only. My offline batch feature builders must reproduce this same prefix-only information restriction at every scored row.

2.2 Prediction target and evaluation metric

For series i, let Hᵢ denote its historical segment and xᵢ,₀:t its observed online prefix. A score sᵢ,t must be measurable with respect to these observations alone. With τᵢ denoting the online change location, the binary target is:

yᵢ,t = 1{τᵢ exists and τᵢ ≤ t}.(1)

At each time t, the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), denoted AUC(t), compares positive and negative series that remain observable. The official pair-weighted metric is [4]:

TS-AUC = Σₜ n₊(t)n₋(t) AUC(t) / Σₜ n₊(t)n₋(t).(2)

A time-only score cannot discriminate within a fixed t. Forecasting negative log-likelihood (NLL), pooled row AUC and time-stratified AUC therefore answer different questions. In particular, a change in a common time prior need not improve this ranking.

2.3 My research partition and derived diagnostics

From the supplied training data, I built a full causal feature cache containing 5,036,517 online rows; sampling every 25th online step yields 206,261 research rows. Historical lengths range from 1,000 to 5,000, with median 2,998. I reserve a fixed 20% of training series for confirmation and use the other 8,000 for search. This 2,000-series holdout is my own research partition, not the organizer's private test set. The separate 100-series reduced test had already been consulted during research.

Retrospective metadata classifies 4,866 break series by their dominant change: 2,572 variance, 1,938 autocorrelation and 356 mean changes. This taxonomy is computed using post-break observations and is used only for evaluation. It does not establish the original domains of the individual series. I neither assume a uniformly financial dataset nor provide retrospective break type, strength or age to the detector.

3 Methodology

3.1 Statistical features and the submission model

The feature bank combines expanding and rolling moments, level and scale contrasts, hypothesis-test statistics, tail indicators, cumulative sum (CUSUM) statistics, autoregressive (AR) changes, generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) states and generalized likelihood ratios (GLRs). Raw and residual-transformed streams are evaluated in parallel. Bayesian information criterion (BIC)-weighted autoregressive models remove predictable mean dynamics; additional variance and Rosenblatt and probability integral transform (PIT) representations provide alternative views.

The historical union152 bank combined raw, whitened, GARCH and GLR information. Removing context columns produced the 144-column training line used in the final student package. More columns were not uniformly beneficial: a 731-column bank lost to smaller nested banks. Likewise, leave-one-family-out importance did not measure a family's standalone value when several families substituted for one another.

A historical forward-selection audit illustrates the interaction: on a repeatedly used local reduced evaluation panel, raw84 scored 0.55170; adding whitened level features raised the local score to 0.62591; adding whitened fit features then raised it to 0.65767. The fit family alone did not improve raw84. All three figures are local research scores, not public leaderboard results or independent confirmation. The 104-feature configuration scoring 0.65767 was never publicly evaluated. The selected submission 46 achieved public TS-AUC 0.6191 with a different configuration and evaluation cohort, so subtracting these scores would not estimate its local-to-public generalization gap.

I used the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) [5] for the main feature classifier and a teacher–student training scheme to soften its binary targets. The teacher is an auxiliary classifier that estimates the probability of a break; the student is the detector trained on a mixture of those probabilities and the observed zero/one labels. This supplies graded training targets rather than treating every labelled row as equally certain. The teacher generates targets during training; the student produces the online predictions.

For each student training row, the teacher prediction qᵢ,t is generated by inner series-level cross-fitting entirely within the outer training pool, so the teacher sees neither that row's series nor the outer validation series and their labels cannot leak into the student's training targets. Soft labels take the form:

ỹᵢ,t = (1 − α)yᵢ,t + αqᵢ,t.(3)

Submission 46 used α=0.5 and five student seeds. Although its package name refers to learning using privileged information [6], ablations did not establish a gain from the additional privileged teacher input. The evidence supported soft-label regularization. A later selected recipe, trial312, uses α=0.14595873, ten leaves and extra trees, with 600 rounds in the matched offline evaluation.

3.2 Learned normal-process model

A two-layer gated recurrent unit (GRU) [7] predicts a one-step mean μ̂ₜ and the logarithm v̂ₜ of the squared scale. Training minimizes a Student-t negative log-likelihood with ν=5 in the frozen v5 recipe. Only normal training material is used: historical segments and, in applicable versions, labelled pre-break online portions of training series. Sampling is proportional to usable length.

Lₜ = ½v̂ₜ + ½(ν+1) log[1 + (xₜ−μ̂ₜ)² / (ν exp(v̂ₜ))].(4)
zₜ = (xₜ−μ̂ₜ) / exp(½v̂ₜ).(5)

Residuals are recentered and rescaled using the model's surprises on the same series' historical tail. Original null features comprise mean/variance and autocorrelation GLRs, mixture and maximum evidence, inferred evidence age, recent residual energy and historical/online likelihood summaries. A separate LightGBM maps these features to a null-derived break score.

The principal combination gives the student weight 0.8 and the null-derived score weight 0.2 for t<500; the student alone is used thereafter. Component scores are percentile-ranked in the local fold evaluations. These fold-relative ranks are part of the offline evaluation convention. Their portable replacement by training-fitted cumulative distribution functions (CDFs), and equivalence under strictly streaming inference, remain necessary checks for a new exported package. Causality of residual features alone does not establish export-equivalence of the blend.

3.3 Nested GRU width selection

For each outer fold, a fixed 25% subset of its training series forms a calibration panel. Widths 64, 128 and 256 are compared using downstream calibration TS-AUC. The selected widths across five outer folds are 128, 64, 128, 256 and 64. These are fold-specific choices, not evidence for a universal width of 256.

Null-classifier training features are generated by four inner cross-fitted GRUs; an outer-training GRU produces the validation features. Thus, label-informed normal-material selection never uses the scored outer series. The selected GRU checkpoints are shared by tree seeds 6, 7 and 8. The seeds vary the downstream fits, not the GRU training realization or the underlying dataset.

3.4 Temporal and multiscale extensions

I preregistered independent changes. Early-off replaces the combination with trial312 before t=100. Late-on retains the original early rule and chooses a late weight from {0,0.1,0.2,0.3} using training-only calibration TS-AUC. Multiscale adds mean, energy, lag-product and likelihood summaries over causal windows of 10, 25, 100 and 250 observations.

A separate adaptive gate uses time, history length, historical null NLL, short/medium residual energy and disagreement between null and student scores. A bounded sigmoid weight is optimized on exact calibration TS-AUC, with regularization and a fixed-rule fallback. The gate is frozen before outer validation. It is evaluated separately from the other changes rather than stacked post hoc.

3.5 Sequential residual accumulation

The final extension operates on the calibrated GRU residuals. A clipping bound is the historical 99th percentile of absolute residuals, constrained to [1,10]. Three bounded statistics represent mean, squared energy and lag-1 residual product. The first online lag product uses the last historical residual.

For statistic T and a fixed tilt λ, history-only empirical normalization defines diagnostic log evidence:

ℓλ,t = λT(zₜ) − log[(1/m) Σⱼ exp{λT(zʰⱼ)}].(6)
log Rλ,t = logaddexp(0, log Rλ,t−1) + ℓλ,t.(7)

The initial log state is −∞. Mean tilts are {−0.5,−0.25,0.25,0.5}; energy tilts are {−0.15,0.15}; lag-product tilts are {−0.25,0.25}. Equal mixtures combine the separate tilted states within each family. I output mixture level, running peak and slopes over 25 and 100 observations, giving twelve additional features. The classifier and fixed blend recipe remain unchanged.

The recursion is motivated by Shiryaev–Roberts (SR) detection [8]. Its theoretical optimality or false-alarm guarantees do not automatically apply: my normalization is empirical and residuals may be dependent. This is a diagnostic evidence representation, not a proved martingale construction.

3.6 Normality, distributional diagnostics and feature contribution

I distinguish Gaussian shape from an unchanged generating process. A normal-history GRU models the pre-break process; it does not assert Gaussian innovations. A stable heavy-tailed series can be non-Gaussian without a break, and a break can preserve Gaussian shape while changing its mean, variance or dependence. Normality is therefore a diagnostic feature, not the break label.

Expanding and rolling standardized moments include skewness and excess kurtosis. The implemented Jarque–Bera (JB) statistic [16] combines them with sample size:

JBₙ = (n/6)[skewₙ² + excess-kurtosisₙ²/4].(8)

The code uses population central moments, neutral higher moments for very short windows, and guards against cancellation when the mean is large relative to the scale. Its classical χ²₂ reference is asymptotic under suitable independent sampling. Serial dependence, estimated residual transforms and repeated overlapping windows prevent me from treating an unadjusted p-value as a calibrated online false-alarm rate. No claim that all histories pass a normality test follows from these features, and no Shapiro–Wilk campaign is established by the saved evidence.

Historical quantile thresholds also support approximate Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS), Cramér–von Mises and tail-weighted Anderson–Darling style deviations of the observed online distribution from its own history. These compare distributions; they are not all Gaussian goodness-of-fit tests. Student-t NLL, residual energy, autocorrelation and historical PIT/Rosenblatt transforms provide complementary model-based checks. An empirical normal-score transform can improve marginal shape while retaining temporal dependence; it is not proof that the transformed observations are independent standard normals. The learned-null history-tail NLL is a fit diagnostic whose downstream TS-AUC must be measured separately.

I use several views of feature contribution: split gain and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) for fitted-model usage, feature correlation for duplication, a SHAP interaction graph for potential non-additivity, elastic-net generalized linear model (GLM) coefficients for a simpler functional form, and refitted out-of-fold (OOF) additions/removals for predictive contribution. They answer different questions. A large split gain does not establish incremental value; a near-zero coefficient does not establish that a tree feature can be deleted; neither observational attribution nor an ablation identifies a causal effect in the original data-generating process.

The historical SHAP graph retained the top 2% of non-meta interaction edges: 21 edges formed one 14-feature component, with 74 singletons. Its component linked historical shape/dependence descriptors to long-window statistics. This describes the sampled fitted model at that threshold, not universal additivity. A coefficient diagnostic consequently added 20 explicit historical-shape × long-window products to the 84-feature GLM input. With five series folds and 1,502,019 sampled rows, four of the resulting 104 columns had very small mean absolute elastic-net coefficients. The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) fits also emitted maximum-iteration warnings; I therefore treat this as a diagnostic rather than a fully converged selection certificate.

3.7 Ablation matrix: small-to-large and large-to-small selection

For a feature set F and family G, denote the score from refitting the same learner on a fixed series split by S(F). The complementary inclusion and exclusion contrasts are:

Δin(G | F) = S(F ∪ G) − S(F); Δout(G | F) = S(F) − S(F ∖ G).(9)

Both are context-dependent. In small-to-large forward selection, I start with a sparse core and measure each candidate addition, then repeat after accepting a family. In large-to-small selection, I start from the full bank and refit after removing one family or a joint block. A family can contribute strongly to a sparse core and be replaceable in a saturated bank. Conversely, two individually dispensable families can become important when removed together. Grouped bootstrap stability and nested selection are needed before exporting a selected subset; the existence of a general framework does not establish that every stage was completed for every bank.

The historical reduced-panel matrix uses the same 600-round binary recipe and common raw84 baseline. Whitened level features add +0.074214 alone; fit features add −0.000708 alone but +0.031760 after level features. Starting from the full152 control, dropping fit features costs approximately 0.02355; dropping whitened CUSUM costs approximately 0.03328; dropping both costs approximately 0.03092. These nonlinear contrasts refute a simple independent ranking. Figure 3 shows the saved additions and available removals; blank cells are unmeasured comparisons, not zeros.

The greedy historical path stopped at raw84 + level_white + fit_white, 104 columns and reduced TS-AUC 0.65767; all remaining additions in the next round lost. This reused reduced panel was a research screen, not an independent confirmation or the final submitted bank. A separate grouped union144 drop-family campaign saved fold signs and gates: for example, removing long-window whitened features reduced pooled OOF score by 0.002257 but did not establish significant harm; removing both tail representations reduced it by 0.003064 and lost on all five folds. Its pooled OOF protocol differs from the historical reduced screen, so I do not merge these scores into one homogeneous matrix.

A later family-score forward build investigated a different selection unit: one learned score per family, rather than the family's original columns. Its construction, results and nesting limitations are detailed below. Complementarity among raw columns and complementarity among family predictions are distinct selection problems.

3.7.1 Family mini-models: one learned feature per family

I trained a small classifier on each feature family and used its break probability as a single new feature. For example, a model receiving only whitened long-window mean, scale and dependence statistics produced one long-window family score. A separate model compressed tail statistics into one tail score. This is supervised compression: the score is learned from training labels, rather than being a simple average of the family's columns or its first principal component. The second-stage learner receives these scores, rather than the complete original feature bank:

uᵍᵢ,t = fᵍ(Xᵍᵢ,t); sᵢ,t = h(uᵍ¹ᵢ,t, …, uᵍᴷᵢ,t, t).(10)

Here Xᵍ contains family g's causal features, fᵍ is its mini-model and h is the combiner. Thus one family becomes one model-derived input feature; this is a family-level stacking experiment. The online-time input lets the combiner change how it uses evidence over time, even though time alone cannot discriminate within a time bucket.

The saved implementation evaluated 24 families: 18 raw/whitened statistical groups, the v5 learned null, Allan and PIT-Allan summaries, detector-score velocity, a Kalman model, and Bolt embeddings. Each mini-model was a binary LightGBM with 15 leaves, at least 200 rows per leaf, learning rate 0.05 and 250 rounds. In each of five outer series folds, four inner folds generated mini-model predictions for combiner training; refitting each mini-model on the outer training pool generated its outer validation inputs. This prevents a family's classifier from supplying its own in-sample training predictions to the final combiner.

Greedy selection started with the null score. Candidate scores with absolute Spearman correlation at least 0.8 to a selected score were skipped. A two-fold series split inside the outer training pool evaluated additions with a 150-round combiner; selection stopped below a gain of 0.0005 or at twelve families. The final combiner used 300 rounds, and outer scores were saved for every prefix of the training-selected order. The terminal prefix, rather than the best outer prefix, defines the result below. Four to six family scores were retained per fold; whitened long- and medium-window families were added in all five folds. Bolt was selected once, which establishes occasional selection rather than a confirmed contribution to the full model.

The scope is narrower than “fully nested” might suggest. The family classifiers were cross-fitted, but upstream null and embedding tables were loaded from precomputed caches; this script does not establish their complete outer-fold independence. The two-fold selection scorer reused the four-fold family predictions without refitting those family learners inside each selection split, so its inner selection scores can be optimistic. The loader also does not exclude the fixed research holdout: this historical grouped training-data screen is not a search-only run or a new holdout confirmation. I therefore report its implementation and negative result without certifying leakage-free independence of the entire hierarchy. The loss is consistent with compression discarding useful within-family interactions or an inadequate capacity/selection recipe; the experiment does not isolate which explanation caused it.

3.8 GLMs, pairwise ranking and selection objectives

Two logistic analyses must be distinguished. The ordinary GLM predicts the row label using standardized features and explicit interaction products, fitted with elastic-net SGD. A historical blend used 85% LightGBM and 15% GLM: TS-AUC 0.6060 versus 0.6053 for its matched LightGBM control, with both half-bootstrap intervals crossing zero. These small diagnostic gains were not accepted.

The later pairwise-logistic blend is a ranking surrogate. I sample positive/negative pairs only at the same online time, allocating the 100,000 sampled pairs in proportion to n₊(t)n₋(t). For score margin m between paired observations and temperature T=0.05, its loss is:

Lpair = mean{log[1 + exp(−m/T)]} + regularization.(11)

A five-coefficient sigmoid gate maps four training-standardized causal covariates—log online length, online/history ratio, first-order autoregressive (AR1)-adjusted effective length and historical null NLL—to a weight bounded by 0.5. An analytic gradient and the bounded limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm (L-BFGS-B) optimize the surrogate. Fit-only nested student predictions are necessary because fitted-on-the-same-data scores would bias gate learning. The evaluated variant loses on average 0.002429 against its student control and 0.004850 against fixed zone_v5; all gates fail. Its historical GRU features also inherit the earlier provenance limitation.

Exact TS-AUC optimization was subsequently tested separately using differential evolution, first for the original null and later for the nested selected-width gate. The later adaptive gate loses 0.003679 against the fixed-rule selected-width combination. Thus neither a more metric-aligned objective nor an additional calibration learner guarantees better outer-fold ranking. My selection hierarchy is: exploratory fit diagnostics and contribution screens; training-only nested configuration choice; frozen outer comparisons across folds/seeds; then budgeted confirmation and streaming parity. Lower NLL alone cannot skip downstream model selection.

3.9 Model families investigated

My model search covered both classifiers on engineered features and models operating on the observation sequence. Tree methods included Random Forest (RF), LightGBM, categorical boosting (CatBoost) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Neural networks (NNs) included feedforward multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), feature-based recurrent neural networks (RNNs), raw-sequence convolutional neural networks (CNNs), temporal convolutional networks (TCNs), and pretrained forecasting encoders. The recurrent branch covered a dense GRU, a dendrite-inspired architecture with separate memories for feature groups, and independently recurrent neural network (IndRNN) cells with independent per-neuron recurrent weights. The dendritic model was my recurrent adaptation of sparse branch-to-output wiring, rather than a reproduction of an unchanged feedforward dendritic network. I also investigated simpler logistic models, reservoir computing and kernel/memory-based alternatives. This inventory describes explored families; differing feature banks, data subsets and validation stages prevent a single fair numerical ranking of every historical run.

3.10 Oracle revisions and what they established

The files named oracle_ceiling contain a sequence of approximate probabilistic models, not a known optimal solution for the unknown DGP. The initial model integrated mean- and variance-shift likelihood ratios over candidate break locations, calibrating population amplitude grids on training folds. Subsequent revisions tested shrinkage of measured amplitudes, maximum rather than additive aggregation across scales, autocorrelation and distribution-shape channels, a training-calibrated break-timing prior, and joint Bayesian online change-point detection (BOCPD)-style marginalization in which channels agreed on the same candidate location. The later whitened-residual channel reused the BIC-AR/GARCH/PIT representation. These revisions tested specific explanations for the gap to the feature classifier; adding a channel or changing its aggregation was not inherently beneficial.

Historical oracle revisionLocal pooled OOF TS-AUCFinding

Two other diagnostics must be kept separate. A time-only prior cannot discriminate among series at a fixed online time under TS-AUC, although a location prior inside joint evidence marginalization can alter the ranking. A variant normalized by a series' eventual total online length used future information and was explicitly labelled a non-causal diagnostic, not an admissible inference feature. Likewise, the later mean-break oracle that knew each evaluated series' true break location was retrospective. None of these constructions supplies the exact DGP or licenses forward-looking predictions. Oracle channels also informed larger feature banks and teacher experiments; the subsequent 731-column nested bank lost to smaller banks, reinforcing that extra approximate oracle information did not automatically improve model selection.

3.11 Blending, stacking and complementary predictions

I investigated three ways to combine models. A probability blend averages their outputs, for example s = w p₁ + (1−w) p₂ with a fixed scalar w. An adaptive blend learns w from causal context and model disagreement. Stacking instead feeds base-model predictions into a second learner; the historical dendritic RNN received the LightGBM prediction as an additional input branch alongside engineered features. Averaging seeds of the same learner, concatenating feature families, and teacher–student soft-label training are related ensemble or representation choices, but are not this prediction-input stacking procedure.

Historical probability sweeps combined LightGBM with RF, CatBoost, XGBoost, a logistic GLM, recurrent networks and kernel/reservoir alternatives. Their saved local screens illustrate the difference between an average gain and confirmed complementarity: a 50/50 CatBoost blend scored 0.6102 against its 0.6053 LightGBM control, and a 50/50 RF blend scored 0.6082 against that same control. Neither passed both half-bootstrap tests; decoupled split/bootstrap retests also rejected these saved blends. The 85/15 GLM blend reached 0.6060 without acceptance. These pooled historical scores belong to their own feature banks and cohorts, rather than the recent submission-46 comparison.

The combined whitening-and-stacking RNN screen used 3,000 series and three group folds. Its recurrent score was 0.5503, versus 0.6067 for LightGBM on the common series; the subsequent blend sweep selected weight 1 on LightGBM, retaining no recurrent contribution. The implementation loaded previously computed LightGBM OOF predictions rather than refitting the base learner inside each recurrent outer-training pool. It also used outer validation during neural epoch evaluation. Accordingly, this historical screen does not establish fully nested, selection-independent stacking performance. OOF predictions exclude their own series during base fitting, but may still depend on the meta-learner's outer validation series unless the base fits are nested within that outer training pool.

Later combination experiments used the trial312 student with a separate residual-feature classifier: fixed 80/20 blending before t=500, training-only late-weight selection, and learned sigmoid gates fitted either to a pairwise-logistic surrogate or exact calibration TS-AUC. The selected-width fixed rule reached mean matched search TS-AUC 0.622489 against 0.619308 for trial312; the exact adaptive rule fell to 0.618810. The historical family-score forward build lost approximately 0.0110 against its submission-46 control (Section 3.7.1). The feature-based TCN ensemble in public submission 49 scored 0.6171, below submission 46's 0.6191. Thus flexible combination did not uniformly improve on a simple fixed rule; recent incremental and fixed-holdout tests remain the basis for judging replacement.

My validation requirement is to generate meta-training predictions by series-level inner cross-fitting within each outer training pool, fit score transforms and combination weights there, then evaluate the frozen combination on the outer validation series. A weight selected on all scored OOF series and tested on those same series is an exploratory sweep. Even a separate weight-selection panel does not repair upstream base-model leakage; independence must hold throughout the hierarchy. The recent nested residual experiments satisfy the recorded group-separation protocol, while their fold-relative percentile transforms still require streaming-export validation (Section 3.2).

3.12 Residual transfer within and across model families

I also asked whether a second learner could explain what a first model missed. Two residual constructions answer different questions. A classifier's training error is r=y−pᴬ, whereas a forecasting null produces an observation innovation e=x−μ̂ᴬ, optionally divided by its predicted scale. The former requires a known training label; the latter can be computed when the next observation arrives. My classifier-correction experiments trained B to predict r from the original causal features and added its predicted correction to A:

rᵢ,t = yᵢ,t − pᴬᵢ,t; sᵢ,t = pᴬᵢ,t + k r̂ᴮᵢ,t.(12)

The true label residual is a training target, not an online input feature. At inference, only B's predicted correction is available. Forecast-residual experiments instead pass observed innovations and their causal summaries into the downstream break classifier. Both can cross model families, but they are not interchangeable with prediction-input stacking or ordinary averaging.

The classifier-residual scripts reused global OOF predictions for A and the same series folds for B. These are historical exploratory screens, not fully nested confirmation. A strict successor would construct A's training predictions entirely within B's outer training pool, select k there, and freeze both stages before outer evaluation. The newer nested GRU route addresses shared-model group separation separately; streaming score transforms and fixed-holdout confirmation remain distinct requirements.

4 Experimental design and statistical analysis

Recent comparisons use five outer series-level folds and tree seeds 6, 7 and 8 on the fixed search universe. Each reported search score is a mean of fold TS-AUCs, subsequently averaged across tree seeds. Trials and feature caches are frozen before evaluation; multiple related methods are not merged after observing their outer-fold results.

For acceptance, I use paired whole-series cluster bootstrap, recomputing the actual TS-AUC after resampling. A project-specific two-half rule requires both corrected confidence intervals for candidate-minus-control to lie above zero. Five bootstrap seeds assess sensitivity to the partition/resampling realization; they do not constitute five independent studies. The general bootstrap principle follows Efron [9]; the two-half acceptance rule is my own conservative operational criterion.

Each later comparison uses 300 resamples per bootstrap seed. Bonferroni correction counts differ by campaign: 12 for the early/late/multiscale tests, 16 for the adaptive gate and 20 for sequential residuals. Therefore gate counts across these campaigns are not directly comparable. These corrections address the declared comparison family, not all accumulated researcher selection.

The fixed 2,000-series holdout has a twenty-evaluation project budget, of which five confirmations are registered. I also assess the previously used reduced panel and five preregistered synthetic process families. Neither is presented as independent real-domain validation. Width and trial312 were selected on the search universe; changing folds and seeds does not remove that historical selection bias.

4.1 Validation and implementation audits

Two major corrections affected earlier local conclusions. First, a reduced scorer used absolute rather than relative online time: earlier RF sanity scores near 0.66 became 0.52054 and 0.52167 after correction. Public scores were unaffected. Second, a teacher/student evaluation reused shared folds. At α=0.5 its score fell from 0.64721 to 0.61743 under nested teacher cross-fitting; at α=0.85 it fell from 0.65423 to 0.61120. Older learned-null caches also required stricter separation of holdout labels from online normal-material censoring.

I check label offsets, group separation, row alignment, reset behavior, prefix invariance and finite outputs. Earlier union152 streaming/batch checks found maximum differences near 1.1×10⁻¹³. A later audit (31 October 2026) of the trial-312 package found streaming and batch scores differing by up to 0.007 (median 0.003) on 298 of 300 series, although all 144 features agree to 1.6×10⁻¹³. The cause is LightGBM's zero split (threshold 10⁻³⁵): incremental updates leave residues near 10⁻¹⁶ where the batch computation gives exactly zero, and the batch computation has such residues of its own, so these rows can follow the other branch. Missing values played no role. Setting values with |x|<10⁻⁹ to zero in both training and serving, and retraining, makes streaming and batch scores identical to floating-point precision on 299 of the 300 series; the remaining series differs by at most 1.1×10⁻⁴. The earlier bound therefore holds for features, not for scores. Earlier union152 packages, including the selected submission, use the same scoring path; the effect on their recorded scores has not been measured. For sequential evidence, future-value perturbations leave prefix features unchanged; long extreme streams remain finite; neutral log-evidence satisfies Rₜ=t+1. Strict graphics processing unit (GPU) checkpoint loading and real feature/classifier smoke tests precede full runs.

4.2 Hyperparameters, search algorithms and GPU likelihood evaluation

Hyperparameterization operates at several levels: per-series null-model likelihood parameters; feature banks and residual transforms; learner capacity and regularization; training-material/window choices; and blend weights. Their objectives differ. GAS-t fitting minimizes history NLL; GRU Optuna initially minimizes validation NLL; LightGBM/soft-label and later width/blend searches target grouped downstream TS-AUC. I record the objective and split for each search rather than treating all optimizer winners as detection improvements.

4.2.2 Per-series likelihood fitting and population search

The GAS-t implementation follows the score-driven framework of Creal, Koopman and Lucas [17]. In my AR1 mean and Student-t scale parameterization, λ is the log squared scale and the scaled likelihood score drives its update:

uₜ² = εₜ² exp(−λₜ); bₜ = (ν+1)uₜ²/(ν+uₜ²) − 1.(13)
λₜ₊₁ = ω + βλₜ + αbₜ; εₜ = xₜ − (c + φxₜ₋₁).(14)

Here b is bounded between −1 and ν. The Student-t squared scale exp(λ) is not its variance: for ν>2 the variance also contains ν/(ν−2). The existing module sometimes calls it log variance; this report states the likelihood parameterization explicitly. GAS is the model family, not a global-search algorithm.

An early twenty-history screen recorded several optimizers, but it cannot rank them. The global methods used a box of ±5 on raw persistence, which caps β at about 0.9923, while unconstrained Nelder–Mead could approach 0.999. Near-zero score coefficients were also less accessible inside that box. The large negative NLL changes in Table S3 are therefore the signature of a narrower feasible set, not a demonstration that differential evolution, dual annealing or TPE cannot fit GAS-t. Nonzero fitted coefficients were sometimes described as “fixing degeneracy”; that is not evidence of a better likelihood. Multi-start Nelder–Mead was kept as a practical local recipe, not as a certified global optimum.

Table S3. Diagnostic of an unequal-domain screen, not a ranking of optimizer quality. Positive values mean lower NLL. Later equal-bound comparisons are the GPU pilot (Appendix D) and the 8,000-series downstream fit (Section 5.5).

Differential evolution mutates/recombines a population [18]; particle swarm optimization (PSO) moves particles toward their own and the population's best locations [19]; dual annealing combines stochastic exploration with local search [20]; TPE uses a surrogate model of promising parameter regions [10]. DE is evolutionary search and is distinct from particle swarm; the older script's broad “swarm-family” wording is imprecise. Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) and genetic algorithms are possible alternatives, but no completed equal-domain runs for them are established by these artifacts.

Comparable optimizer evidence begins only when the search domain is shared. I therefore ran a bounded GAS-t GPU pilot. The full-history recurrence runs in a 64-bit floating-point (FP64) kernel using the Heterogeneous-computing Interface for Portability (HIP), parallel over 128 parameter candidates while remaining sequential within each history. Eight fixed search-only histories are evaluated with seeds 6/7/8, 100 generations of DE/rand/1/bin (mutation factor F=0.7, crossover probability 0.8) and particle swarm (inertia 0.7298, cognitive/social 1.49618), plus bounded local restart controls and L-BFGS-B polishing. Both population methods receive the same local anchor; their reported run time excludes the common central processing unit (CPU) anchor cost. All selected NLLs are re-evaluated with the original CPU objective. Expanded raw parameter bounds are identical across these new methods, and no labels or online observations enter this fit. Figure 6 and Appendix D report the completed eight-history pilot. A finite population search does not certify the global optimum. I subsequently tested downstream residual features on all 8,000 search series, with the separate design and results below.

The downstream experiment fits every series using its own history only, without shared fitted parameters or label-dependent censoring. Four bounded Nelder–Mead starts, their local polish, and DE plus polish share the same bounds. Unlike the eight-history pilot, all methods additionally require β−α(ν+1)/4>−0.99: this bounds the lower derivative of the log-scale recursion, while its upper derivative is β<0.999. The restriction was introduced after an extreme-parameter smoke test exposed numerical sensitivity. Hence the full experiment evaluates a modified stable domain, not a simple enlargement of the pilot cohort. The AR(1) coefficient remains restricted to [−0.5,0.5].

A single fixed optimization seed 6 and 128 candidates over 100 generations determine the per-history DE fits. A continuous fitted-initial-scale recursion processes history and the online prefix; the last 500 historical residuals calibrate mean/scale. Eleven causal change-evidence and likelihood summaries feed five-fold LightGBM classifiers with tree seeds 6/7/8 and 600 rounds. The frozen combination uses 80% trial 312 and 20% GAS-derived score before t=500, then trial 312 alone. Controls reproduce the same IDs, times, targets and folds. Seven declared comparisons per tree seed, five bootstrap seeds and 300 resamples yield 105 gates, with two-sided corrected intervals at α=0.05/7. This does not correct for all historical research reuse or constitute three independent optimizer realizations.

Tree size, seed averaging and burn-in also require context. Figure 4 reports a historical round curve, same-seed tree-capacity comparisons, individually measured seeds versus their probability average, and online ratchet burn-in. Online burn-in delays score smoothing; AR burn-in makes order likelihoods comparable; optimizer startup and neural warm-up are separate concepts. Increasing rounds or averaging predictions is not selecting the best validation seed. Early stopping on sparse cross-validation (CV), reduced-panel rankings and public scores must remain separate: their misalignment motivated nested controls and exported-package checks.

DE plus polish improves its matched blend by 0.000866 over local polish alone and wins 9/15 fold–seed cells. Against trial 312 the mean gain is 0.001368 with 11/15 wins; against submission 46 it is 0.006661 with 12/15 wins. However, it trails the selected-width GRU combination by 0.001813 and sequential GRU evidence by 0.002548, winning only 6/15 and 3/15 cells respectively. The standalone null classifier scores 0.562205 versus 0.559395 under local polish, but that comparison also fails every gate. A better raw likelihood does not determine which residual representation best complements the student.

On the same 8,000 histories, DE lowers summed whole-history NLL by a mean 7.226998 relative to unpolished local fits and 3.198186 relative to local polish. At tolerance 10⁻⁶ it beats local polish on 3,521 histories and loses on 1,849; the remaining 2,630 are within tolerance. These are sums over each complete history, not per-observation forecasting losses, and cannot be compared numerically with the GRU's 1.283579 validation objective. The population includes the unpolished local anchor, making non-regression against that anchor a protocol property rather than proof of global optimality. Local polish was not itself injected as the DE anchor, so it can still beat the finite population search.

For DE blend versus local-polish blend, tree seed 6/bootstrap seed 0 gives half-sample deltas +0.000357 and +0.001303 with corrected intervals [−0.003414, +0.004348] and [−0.001431, +0.004126]. Both include zero. The 105 failures therefore preserve the distinction between a positive average and accepted evidence; failure is not proof of zero benefit. These resamples condition on the saved predictions, rather than refitting the full model hierarchy. As in earlier campaigns, 300 resamples provide limited resolution at the corrected tails.

The controller initially misclassified completion because a PowerShell process refresh returned a null exit code, skipping the automatic audit. The frozen computation and all three seed result files were complete. I performed the audit manually and corrected the controller's process-handle handling without altering scientific sources or rerunning the experiment. The source/input provenance and recovery records are retained separately. The frozen implementation, audit, predictions and code review are retained in src/gas_t_downstream_validation.py and artifacts/gas_t_downstream_validation/.

Detection diagnostics use the top 20% scores within each fold/time cross-section. Among break series with sufficient scored follow-up, detection within 25 observations is 20.17% for selected-width null, 20.51% for multiscale and 20.59% for sequential residuals. I also save within-50/100 detection, pre-break alarms and never-break ever-alarm rates. These are relative-rank diagnostics, not deployed thresholds or calibrated false-alarm probabilities. Delays are quantized by step25 sampling, and ever-alarm rates depend on exposure.

A mean-break oracle using the true change location scored about 0.663 on a retrospective panel, while existing mean statistics were already near 0.67. This is a comparison with that oracle construction, not a mathematical upper bound. A nested mean-specialist blend was subsequently rejected, supporting caution about another mean-only detector.

The GAS result is heterogeneous across online phases. The DE blend improves on its local-polish control in all three pre-cutoff buckets, yet only the earliest bucket beats the stronger GRU combinations. This helps explain why better history fitting yields a weaker aggregate detector than the existing sequential GRU route.

These retrospective findings were not used to retune the evaluated combination.

7 Discussion and limitations

The completed GAS experiment reinforces the separation between fit and task performance: broader history-likelihood search improved its own residual blend but did not beat the existing GRU combinations or pass acceptance. Its early advantage and middle-phase loss suggest context-specific complementarity; this was not independently validated or used to retune the frozen rule. Table S3 still cannot support a ranking of global search algorithms, because those historical runs used a tighter persistence box than Nelder–Mead. The later DE comparison is only within a shared, stability-restricted domain, with one optimizer seed, a fixed temporal cutoff and fold-relative ranks. Those limits, together with the restricted AR1/Student-t null, prevent a general verdict about GAS or about global optimization.

The strongest practical contribution of the submitted model was the combination of complementary representations and nested soft-label regularization. Separate learned residuals subsequently added useful search signal. Sequential accumulation yielded the largest recent average search score and addressed part of the early deficit, but did not achieve broad fold consistency or incremental statistical acceptance.

Three limits are central. First, extensive reuse of the search universe creates selection bias that new seeds and stricter cross-fitting cannot remove. Second, sparse local scoring and fold-relative percentile blends are not complete streaming-export validation. Third, the newest representations lack fixed-holdout confirmation and independent domain tests. The rounded older holdout gains cannot be assigned to the later residual model.

The acceptance rule is conservative. Failure means that the chosen procedure did not establish a positive effect in both halves; it is not proof of zero benefit. At the same time, lowering the threshold after seeing failures would weaken the evidential standard. I therefore preserve both the numerical improvements and the non-acceptance verdict.

Between 14 and 28 October 2026 I ran no new detector comparison on the ADIA search folds and used no further fixed-holdout evaluation. Five of the twenty fixed-holdout evaluations have been spent; fifteen remain. (Corrected 30 October 2026: v1.0 stated that five remained.)

Compared with previous-edition solution reports [3], the main methodological difference is availability of data at prediction time. Complete post-boundary segment comparisons and their ROC-AUC cannot be transferred directly to unknown-location causal monitoring. A 2025 winning score near 0.90 is not a target against which my 0.6191 TS-AUC submission should be ranked.

8 Conclusion

The selected submission achieved recorded public TS-AUC 0.6191. On the organisers' final private test set of 10,000 series it scored 0.6196, rank 239 of 819 scored models (first place 0.6935, tenth place 0.6686; Crunch Lab results announcement, October 2026). Public and private scores differ by 0.0005, so the selection did not overfit the public leaderboard. Offline development increased a matched local control from 0.614015 to 0.623224 using a student, nested learned-null model and sequential residual evidence. The last extension improves early ranking but loses some middle-phase performance and fails incremental acceptance gates. The separate full 8K GAS-t likelihood-search test yields 0.620676, below the GRU routes, with all 105 gates failing. Improved likelihood alone has not produced an accepted successor. These results identify a promising representation and clarify the validation requirements for a successor; they do not establish a production replacement or improved private leaderboard result.
